newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Results drive Ericsson to new peak.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Results drive Ericsson to new peak.

text.p: Swedish telecoms group AB LM Ericsson posted a surprise 44 percent leap in first half pre-tax earnings on Thursday, sparking a buying spree that sent the company's share soaring to a record high.

Pre-tax profits of 6.10 billion crowns for the first half of 1997 was more than one billion crowns higher than market consensus estimates and the share soared over 10 percent before stabilising at 361 crowns, up 32 crowns.
The company said mobile telephone sales rocketed more than 100 percent in the period and its global market share in the first half of this year rose to 16 percent from 12 percent a year ago.
Ericsson chief executive Lars Ramqvist said falling prices for mobile telephones, which analysts say is a concern as competition in the sector grows, was surprisingly small.

"On the whole we have managed to keep our margins in good shape. Price stability on mobile telephones has been better than we thought and increased volumes coupled with good margins has given us a good profit," Ramqvist told Reuters.
Net sales for the group amounted to 72.21 billion crowns in the period, a 44 percent increase on the first half of 1996.

Its mobile telephones unit posted sales of 18.39 billion crowns compared to 9.09 billion. Sales for its mobile infrastructure division, its largest business area, jumped to 30.10 billion crowns from 23.45 billion.
In its public telecoms unit, Infocom Systems, sales rose to 21.47 billion crowns from 15.95 billion.
Lehman Brothers analyst Jeremy Alun-Jones said the numbers looked healthy.
"The sales were about 10 percent better than we expected. We will probably raise our EPS estimates by about 10 percent for 1997," he said.
Ramqvist said the result of the Infocom Systems operations was still not up to par. He said he expected a turnaround for the unit in 1997 and its result to be satisfactory in 1998.
Some analysts voiced concern about the company's growing reliance on mobile handsets, which have lower margins than the mobile infrastructure business.
"Ericsson is becoming more similar to companies like Nokia as it becomes more dependent on mobile phones than systems," said Aros Securities chief analyst Lars Larsen.
"You have to consider if this will effect the way you value the company," Larsen added.
